name: T. H. Green
dossier: Whyte's Professor of Moral Philosophy at Oxford, and a Liberal in city politics. The Lectures on the Principles of Political Obligation, published from his papers, argue that rights exist among persons who recognise a common good, and that will, not mere force, is the basis of the state.
voice: I ask whether this recognises persons in a common good.

works.title: Lectures on the Principles of Political Obligation
works.note: From the Philosophical Works, volume II. Public domain.

entries.claim: They make no inquiry into the development of society and of man through society.
entries.work: Lectures on the Principles of Political Obligation
entries.loc: G. Will, not force, is the basis of the state
entries.bears: He faults contract theories for ignoring how persons and society develop together.
entries.modern: They make no inquiry into the development of society and of man through society. He faults contract theories for ignoring how persons and society develop together.

entries.claim: A right is a power claimed and recognised as contributory to a common good.
entries.work: Lectures on the Principles of Political Obligation
entries.loc: A. The grounds of political obligation
entries.bears: A right, on this account, is a recognised power that serves a common good.
entries.modern: A right is a power claimed and recognised as contributory to a common good. A right, on this account, is a recognised power that serves a common good.

entries.claim: A right against society, in distinction from a right to be treated as a member of society, is a contradiction in terms.
entries.work: Lectures on the Principles of Political Obligation
entries.loc: A. The grounds of political obligation
entries.bears: He will not separate a right from membership in the society that recognises it.
entries.modern: A right against society, in distinction from a right to be treated as a member of society, is a contradiction in terms. He will not separate a right from membership in the society that recognises it.

entries.claim: No one therefore can have a right except (1) as a member of a society, and (2) of a society in which some common good is recognised by the members of the society as their own ideal good, as that which should be for each of them.
entries.work: Lectures on the Principles of Political Obligation
entries.loc: A. The grounds of political obligation
entries.bears: A right, on this account, is not a claim one person holds against every society.
entries.modern: No one therefore can have a right except (1) as a member of a society, and (2) of a society in which some common good is recognised by the members of the society as their own ideal good, as that which should be for each of them. A right, on this account, is not a claim one person holds against every society.

entries.claim: Conversely, everyone capable of being determined by the conception of a common good as his own ideal good, as that which unconditionally should be (of being in that sense an end to himself), in other words, every moral person, is capable of rights; i.e. of bearing his part in a society in which the free exercise of his powers is secured to each member through the recognition by each of the others as entitled to the same freedom with himself.
entries.work: Lectures on the Principles of Political Obligation
entries.loc: A. The grounds of political obligation
entries.bears: Freedom here is a freedom people secure for one another by recognition.
entries.modern: Conversely, everyone capable of being determined by the conception of a common good as his own ideal good, as that which unconditionally should be (of being in that sense an end to himself), in other words, every moral person, is capable of rights; i.e. of bearing his part in a society in which the free exercise of his powers is secured to each member through the recognition by each of the others as entitled to the same freedom with himself. Freedom here is a freedom people secure for one another by recognition.

entries.claim: Laws of this kind have often been objected to on the strength of a one-sided view of the function of laws; the view, viz., that its only business is to prevent interference with the liberty of the individual.
entries.work: Lectures on the Principles of Political Obligation
entries.bears: He thinks a law can do more than stand out of the way.
entries.modern: Laws of this kind have often been objected to on the strength of a one-sided view of the function of laws; the view, viz., that its only business is to prevent interference with the liberty of the individual. He thinks a law can do more than stand out of the way.

entries.claim: He regards the state (πόλις) as a society of which the life is maintained by what its members do for the sake of maintaining it, by functions consciously fulfilled with reference to that end, and which in that sense imposes duties; and at the same time as a society from which its members derive the ability, through education and protection, to fulfil their several functions, and which in that sense confers rights.
entries.work: Lectures on the Principles of Political Obligation
entries.bears: Education and protection are, in the account he is following, how a state confers the ability to do one's part.

Education and protection are, in the account he is following, how a state confers the ability to do one's part.

entries.claim: E.g. in the American war of secession, though it would be difficult to say that a man had not as much a right to fight for his seceding state as for the Union, yet as the special interest of the seceding states was that of maintaining slavery, there was reason for holding that the side of the Union, not that of the seceding states, was the one which ought to be taken.
entries.work: Lectures on the Principles of Political Obligation
entries.loc: On war and the common good
entries.bears: He will judge a war by the good it serves, and he names slavery as deciding this one.

entries.claim: A son, when by the death of his father according to Roman law he was delivered from 'patria potestas' and became in turn head of a family, acquired a 'persona' which he had not before, the 'persona' which had previously belonged to the father.
entries.work: Lectures on the Principles of Political Obligation
entries.bears: Legal personality, in the example he uses, can be something a household confers rather than something one simply has.
